STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
CITY OF TRENTON,
Respondent,
-and- Docket No. CO-2026-118
PBA LOCAL 11A, SUPERIOR OFFICERS
ASSOCIATION (SOA),
Charging Party.
SYNOPSIS
The Commission denies PBA Local 11A (SOA)’s motion for
reconsideration seeking interim relief (IR), dismisses its charge
alleging a refusal to negotiate in good faith, and remands for
complaint issuance and further processing of its claim alleging
interference with statutory rights, in the SOA’s unfair practice
charge (UPC) against the City of Trenton. The UPC alleges the
City violated the Act when its Police Director sent an email
accusing the SOA President of extortion and other
unlawful/improper activity during negotiations. The IR
application sought a retraction of the email pending final
disposition of the UPC. The Commission sustains the denial of
IR, finding the SOA did not establish irreparable harm where the
requested retraction may be ordered as part of an overall remedy
at the conclusion of the proceeding, and there is recourse for
appeal of discipline imposed for protected activity resulting
from any express or implied threat contained within the email.
However, the Commission finds further processing of the
interference charge is required to determine whether the Police
Director’s accusations lacked a legitimate and substantial
business justification. Finally, the Commission finds no basis
for complaint issuance on the alleged refusal to negotiate
because the email contains no such explicit refusal nor any
assertion by the Police Director that the matters under
discussion were not negotiable.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

DECISION

reconsideration of a decision issued on January 14 by the
Director of Unfair Practices (Director), denying the PBA’s
request for interim relief (IR) on its unfair practice charge
(UPC) against the City of Trenton (City).
As filed on December 30, 2025, together with its IR request,
the PBA’s UPC alleges the City violated sections 5.4a(1), (3),
(4), and (5) of the New Jersey Employer-Employee Relations Act
(Act), N.J.S.A. 34:13A-1 et seq.1/, when its Police Director sent

an official written accusation of

In support of its motion for reconsideration and its
response to the defect letter, the SOA filed a brief, exhibits,
the supplemental certification of President J.W., and the
certification of Captain J.S., an SOA member who serves as the
Police Director’s Chief of Staff. The Commission received no
responsive filing from the City. These facts appear.
J.W. certifies that the parties are in negotiations for a
successor to their most recent collective negotiations agreement
(CNA) governing superior officers’ terms and conditions of
employment that expired on December 31, 2023. That CNA includes
a 4% compensation differential commonly referred to, J.W.
certifies, as “detective pay” or the “detective differential.”
He further certifies that this differential has been applied in
practice to certain atypical investigative or confidential
assignments, where the assignment is not a traditional case-
carrying “detective” role.
J.W. certifies that in October of 2024 the SOA submitted a
written contract proposal to the City’s negotiator, its Business
Administrator, that included a 4% stipend for the SOA President,
in lieu of a detective differential. In 2025, J.W. pursued
“administrative discussions” with various City representatives
(including the Mayor, the Mayor’s Chief of Staff, and the

Business Administrator) about the proposed SOA President stipend
as well as a separate proposal for a stipend for the title of
Public Information Officer (PIO), which was also based on “the
existing detective differential framework.” J.W. certifies that
he followed up on these discussions relating to the stipend
proposals with supporting documentation sent by email to the
Business Administrator on November 6, 2025.
The Police Director’s email that is the subject of this
dispute recounts a meeting that took place in his office on
November 7, 2025, when J.W. arrived, according to the email, “to
have a conversation” about “the contract situation between the
city and the unions (PBA & SOA)”. Dated November 13, the email
was sent to legal counsel for both the SOA and the City as well
as to President J.W. and Captain J.S., among others. It states
that the Police Director’s Chief of Staff, J.S., was also
initially present at the meeting until J.W. asked to speak
privately with the Police Director, whereupon J.S. exited the
room. The charge focuses on allegations in the email about a
conversation between the Police Director and J.W., after J.S.

President [J.W.] then advised me that he felt
I should give him detective pay and expressed
the reasons why. I initially scoffed at the
idea but agreed I would hear him out. I
advised him that detective pay was only given
because one was doing detective work or one
was assigned to the Director’s Office. He
didn’t agree, offering different reasons that
are outside of the contract or past practice

As I am not willing to engage in Quid Pro Quo

assume that this is the unfair labor practice
for which he was trying to solicit unearned
detective pay?

the stipend proposal as a criminal act of “extortion” or “illegal

Analysis
Motion for Reconsideration of IR Denial
Motions for reconsideration of interim relief decisions are
governed by N.J.A.C. 19:14-9.6, which states, in pertinent part:
Reconsideration will only be granted based on
a demonstration of extraordinary
circumstances and exceptional importance.
The movant shall specify and bear the burden
of establishing the grounds warranting
reconsideration. . . . The filing and
pendency of a motion for reconsideration
shall not operate to stay the effectiveness
of the Commission’s designee’s interim relief
decision unless otherwise ordered by the
Commission.
Only in cases of exceptional importance will we intrude into the
regular interim relief process by granting a motion for
reconsideration by the full Commission. City of Passaic,
P.E.R.C. No. 2004-50, 30 NJPER 67 (&21 2004); Borough of Closter,
P.E.R.C. No. 2001-75, 27 NJPER 289 (&32104 2001). Interim relief
is an extraordinary remedy to be invoked only in limited
circumstances where appropriate and necessary. State of New
Jersey, P.E.R.C. No. 76-6, 1 NJPER 41 (1975).
To obtain interim relief, the moving party must demonstrate
that it has a substantial likelihood of prevailing in a final
Commission decision on its legal and factual allegations and that
irreparable harm will occur if the requested relief is not

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 10.
granted. Further, the public interest must not be injured by an
interim relief order and the relative hardship to the parties in
granting or denying relief must be considered. Crowe v. De
Gioia, 90 N.J. 126, 132-134 (1982); State of New Jersey (Stockton
State College), P.E.R.C. No. 76-6, 1 NJPER 41 (1975); Little
Egg Harbor Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 94, 1 NJPER 37 (1975). A party
seeking such relief “has the burden to prove each of the Crowe
factors by clear and convincing evidence.” Garden State Equality
v. Dow, 216 N.J. 314, 320 (2013)(emphasis added); Essex Cty.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2005-56, 31 NJPER 103, 106 and n.2 (P45 2005)(all
elements of Crowe test must be present).
Applying the above standards to the record presented, we
deny the SOA’s motion for reconsideration. We sustain the denial
of interim relief because we agree with the Director that the SOA
has not established that it will suffer irreparable harm if the
requested relief is not granted. Harm becomes irreparable in
circumstances where the Commission cannot fashion an adequate
remedy which would return the parties to the conditions that
existed before the occurrence of any unfair practice at the
conclusion of the processing of the unfair practice charge.
Camden Cty. Bd. of Chosen Freeholders, P.E.R.C. No. 2020-60, 47
NJPER 32 (¶6 2020) (citing, City of Newark, I.R. No. 2006-3, 31
NJPER 250 (¶97 2005); Atlantic City Bd. of Ed., I.R. No. 2003-14,
29 NJPER 305 (¶94 2003); and Sussex Cty., I.R. No. 2003-13, 29
NJPER 274 (¶81 2003)).

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 11.
The interim relief sought by the SOA is a retraction of the
Police Director’s November 13 email pending the outcome of the
UPC. If it is determined at the conclusion of the processing of
the UPC that the email violated the Act, such a retraction may be
ordered as part of the overall remedy, thus returning the parties
to conditions that existed before the commission of the unfair
practice.
Further, even assuming (without deciding) that the Police
Director’s email contains an express or implied threat of
discipline for protected activity, the imposition of such
discipline would not constitute irreparable harm where there is
recourse for appeal of that discipline. See, City of Trenton,
I.R. No. 2005-7, 31 NJPER 28 (¶13 2005)(denying IR where “no
discipline had been imposed” on PBA president, “he was still
working and available to represent” employees, and “a
sophisticated [Civil Service] appeal procedure” existed to decide
the legitimacy of then-preliminary disciplinary charges that were
allegedly in retaliation for protected activity). See also,
Bergen Community College, I.R. No. 2008-10, 34 NJPER 58 (¶22
2008) (threat or imposition of discipline does not constitute
irreparable harm); State of New Jersey, I.R. No. 2007-14, 33
NJPER 138 (¶49 2007)(same), recon. granted on other grounds,
P.E.R.C. No. 2008-12, 33 NJPER 225 (¶85 2007); Allentown Bor.,
I.R. No. 2001-14, 27 NJPER 264 (¶32094 2001)(same); Sayreville
Bor., I.R. No. 93-14, 19 NJPER 166 (¶24083 1993)(same). Here,
such disciplinary appeal procedures are available to the SOA,

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 12.
through either the parties’ negotiated grievance procedure (minor
discipline) or the Civil Service (major discipline), as the City
of Trenton is a Civil Service municipality. Trenton City Code,
Art. III, §2-8(A)(1).
Pleading Defects
For purposes of administrative efficiency, we will also
consider whether the SOA’s response to the Director’s January 15
letter has cured any pleading defects. N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1(a)
sets forth the Commission’s unfair practice complaint issuance
standard, in pertinent part as follows:
[I]f it appears to the Director of Unfair
Practices that the allegations of the charge,
if true, may constitute unfair practices on
the part of the respondent, and that formal
proceedings should be instituted in order to
afford the parties an opportunity to litigate
relevant legal and factual issues, the
Director shall issue and serve a formal
complaint.
[N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1(a) (emphasis added).]
Our rules also provide that before a complaint issues, the
Director “may permit the charging party to amend a charge upon
such terms as may be deemed just.” N.J.A.C. 19:14-1.5(a).
The SOA responded to the defect letter with an amended UPC
that (on the present record) does not seek complaint issuance on
the section 5.4a(3) and 5.4a(4) claims set forth in its initial
charge. The SOA also provided additional facts and legal
argument. As further explained below, we find the SOA has

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 13.
satisfied the complaint issuance standard as to its section
5.4a(1) claims, but not its 5.4a(5) claim.
The 5.4a(1) Claim
An employer independently violates section 5.4a(1) if its
action tends to interfere with an employee’s statutory rights and
lacks a legitimate and substantial business justification.
Somerville Bd. of Ed., D.U.P. No. 2024-18, 51 NJPER 59, 60 (¶15
2024); N.J. Sports & Exposition Auth., P.E.R.C. No. 80-73, 5
NJPER 550, n.1 (¶10285 1979)). Proof of actual interference,
intimidation, restraint, coercion, or motive is unnecessary; the
objective tendency to interfere is sufficient. Id. (citing,
Commercial Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 83-25, 8 NJPER 550
(¶13253 1982), aff’d 1983 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 5 (App. Div.
1983); City of Hackensack, P.E.R.C. No. 78-71, 4 NJPER 190 (¶4096
1978), aff’d 1979 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 11 (App. Div. 1979)).
A violation of another unfair practice provision derivatively
violates subsection 5.4a(1). See, e.g., Lakehurst Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2004-74, 30 NJPER 186 (¶69 2004), aff’d, 2005 N.J.
Super. Unpub. LEXIS 841 (App. Div. 2005).
Section 5.4a(1) cases require a balancing of two important
but conflicting rights: the employer’s right of free speech and
the employees’ rights to be free from coercion, restraint or
interference in the exercise of protected rights. State of N.J.
(Trenton State Coll.), P.E.R.C. No. 88-19, 13 NJPER 720 (¶18269
1987). In striking that balance, all circumstances of a
particular case must be reviewed. Id. An employer has the right

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 14.
to criticize an employee representative as long as the employer’s
actions do not rise to the level of unlawful interference with
protected rights. Black Horse Pike Reg. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No.
82-19, 7 NJPER 502 (¶12223 1981). “Unflattering descriptions,
although unfortunate, are sometimes part of both the work and the
labor relations environment. They are not, however, necessarily
illegal.” Lakehurst Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2004-74, 30 NJPER
186 (¶69 2004), aff’d 31 NJPER 290 (¶113 App. Div. 2005).
The City, having filed no response to the SOA’s IR
application, its motion for reconsideration, or its response to
the defect letter, did not place into the record a legitimate and
substantial business justification for the accusatory statements
in the Police Director’s November 13 email. Nor has the City
disputed the SOA’s certified statements. These include the SOA
President’s view that given his position of authority the Police
Director’s accusation of illegal and unethical conduct created
professional jeopardy for J.W. as a law enforcement officer and
the foreseeable risk of referral for disciplinary action; and
Captain J.S.’s certified opinion that the Police Director’s
accusations against J.W. did not warrant an official inquiry,
Internal Affairs report, or criminal referral.
Further, there is no claim or evidence that J.W. was not
acting in his official capacity as SOA President during the
November 7 meeting, or that the matters under discussion in that
meeting did not concern negotiations over negotiable terms and
conditions of employment. See, e.g., Hamilton Tp. Bd. of Ed.,

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 15.
D.U.P. No. 82-24, 8 NJPER 199 (¶13083 1982) (refusing to issue
complaint on unit members’ charge that association violated its
duty of fair representation when it negotiated multi-year
contract which required withdrawal of certain unfair practice
charges in exchange for certain employer concessions).
Although the Police Director evidently holds a civilian
position, the City’s Administrative Code makes him “directly
responsible for the efficient and routine day-to-day operations
of the Police Department”, with authority to “[a]dopt and
promulgate rules and regulations for the government of the
divisions under his/her supervision and for the discipline of
their members.” Trenton City Code, Art. XII, §2-57(C)(emphasis
added). In light of this significant authority, including over
police disciplinary matters, we find that the allegations in the
SOA’s amended charge, if true, may constitute unfair practices on
the part of the respondent, supporting the issuance of a
complaint under 5.4a(1). That is, further processing of the
charge is required to determine whether the Police Director’s
accusations of illegal and unethical conduct against the SOA
President lacked any legitimate and substantial business
justification.
The 5.4a(5) Claim
The Commission’s standard for determining whether a party
has refused to negotiate in good faith in violation of Section
5.4a(5) of the Act is as follows:

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 16.
It is necessary to subjectively analyze the
totality of the parties’ conduct in order to
determine whether an illegal refusal to
negotiate may have occurred. A determination
that a party has refused to negotiate in good
faith will depend upon an analysis of the
overall conduct and/or attitude of the party
charged. The object of this analysis is to
determine the intent of the respondent, i.e.,
whether the respondent brought to the
negotiating table an open mind and a sincere
desire to reach an agreement, as opposed to a
predetermined intention to go through the
motions, seeking to avoid, rather than reach,
an agreement.
[State of New Jersey, 1 NJPER 39, 40 (1975),
aff’d 141 N.J. Super. 470 (App. Div. 1976).]
Applying that standard here, we find the Police Director’s email
does not evidence a refusal to negotiate requiring the issuance
of a complaint under 5.4a(5). While further processing of the
charge is warranted under 5.4a(1) as detailed supra, the email
contains no explicit refusal to negotiate nor, as the SOA admits,
any assertion by the Police Director to the effect that the
matters under discussion are not negotiable.
The SOA’s certifications do not refute or take specific
issue with the email’s statements that the Police Director agreed
to “hear out” J.W. regarding the proposed stipend for the SOA
President and expressing the Police Director’s view that
“detective pay was only given because one was doing detective
work or one was assigned to the Director’s Office.” The email
further contains the Police Director’s opinion that the reasons
offered by J.W in support of the stipend “are outside of the

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 17.
contract or past practice for awarding detective pay.” Overall,
we find that while these statements indicate the parties had
differing viewpoints about the proposal, they are not
inconsistent with good-faith negotiations and do not evince a
“predetermined intention to go through the motions” or avoid,
rather than reach, an agreement.
ORDER
Based upon the foregoing, SOA’s motion for reconsideration
is denied, its 5.4a(5) charge is dismissed, and the matter is
remanded to the Director for complaint issuance and further
processing of its 5.4a(1) claim.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Davey, Eaton, Higgins, and
Hines voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
